reason: I'll start building bone: the fibres bend and the mineral resists squeezing, so together they seem useful for strength.
expectation: I expect a bone material combining flexible fibres with hard mineral, though it may still need living cells and blood vessels.

alternatives.reason: The lining clearly fits the sleeve, but I want to build the bone first.

effect: The fibres now have mineral among them, but the bone still needs living cells and a blood supply.
reaction: It makes sense that the fibres and mineral contribute different kinds of strength.
reason: I'll combine the bone cells and blood vessels to work toward living, supplied bones; the picture shows channels connecting cells toward a vessel.
expectation: I expect bone cells connected to a blood supply, though I don't know exactly how they'll join the reinforced fibres.

alternatives.reason: The joint lining fits the sleeve, but I want to continue with the bone first.

effect: The picture shows nutrients reaching bone cells through tiny channels, so I can now add the supplied cells to the reinforced fibres.
reaction: The distinction between nutrients leaving the vessel and blood cells staying inside is helpful.
reason: Combining the supplied cells with the reinforced fibres should finish the living bone project.
expectation: I expect living arm bones containing the reinforced fibres and cells supplied by blood vessels.

alternatives.reason: The joint sleeve also needs its lining, but I want to finish the bone first.

effect: The living arm bones are complete, and the new goal is a supported movable joint.
reaction: It is satisfying to see the cells, vessels and strong material together in the bone.
reason: The cartilage caps cover the facing bone ends and help them slide, so adding them is a useful start on the movable joint.
expectation: I expect arm bones with smooth cartilage covering their joint surfaces; they will probably still need the sleeve and ligaments.

alternatives.reason: The lining fits inside the sleeve, but I want to prepare the bone ends first.

effect: The bone ends now have smooth cartilage caps; the joint still needs its lined sleeve.
reaction: The result matches the picture of surfaces prepared to slide.
reason: The lining fits inside the sleeve and produces joint fluid. This is the only offered combination.
expectation: I expect a fluid-lined joint sleeve that can later surround the capped bone ends.

effect: The sleeve now has a lining and fluid-filled space, so it is ready to join the capped bones.
reaction: The picture helps show how the sleeve surrounds the joint while the cartilage surfaces remain separate.
reason: This is the only offered combination and brings the prepared bone ends and sleeve together.
expectation: I expect a fluid-lined joint around the cartilage-capped bones; it may still need ligaments for support.

effect: The capped bones are now enclosed in the fluid-lined sleeve; ligaments remain to support the joint.
reaction: The explanation makes the roles of cartilage and joint fluid clear.
reason: The ligaments connect bones and resist sideways separation. This is the only offered combination.
expectation: I expect a supported elbow joint that can move without the bones slipping apart.

effect: The ligaments complete the supported, movable elbow, and all goals are finished.
reaction: Seeing the elbow bend with its parts in place is satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Putting the supplied cells and reinforced fibres together made it clear that bone is both strong material and living tissue.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding the sleeve to the capped bones felt a little repetitive after preparing both parts, though it completed an understandable step.

surprise.text: The picture of nutrients passing through tiny channels to bone cells helped me understand how living cells are supplied inside bone.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures gave the parts clear jobs, even when there was only one offered combination.

continue.text: Yes. Building the elbow made the parts' jobs understandable, and I'd be curious to see how movement connects to muscles in another chapter.
